chunk-001:c008.proposition: Determinism does not eliminate the responsibility-relevant ability to do otherwise because people remain capable of responding to persuasion, changing their conduct, and developing moral competence.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source independently identifies observable changeability and responsiveness to persuasion as practical capacities that determinism does not prevent, supplying a standalone compatibilist account of alternatives.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-03.proposition: Basic moral desert is a misleading requirement, while sufficient ordinary moral responsibility can still justify coercion, imprisonment, fines, and reputational consequences for violations.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source affirmatively distinguishes an unnecessary basic-desert construct from sufficient ordinary responsibility and identifies concrete consequences that the latter can justify.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-06.proposition: Deterministic causation does not eliminate accountable sourcehood because autonomous agents become largely self-made through sustained learning, reflection, practice, exposure to reasons, and moral education.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source supplies a positive developmental basis for autonomy: agents form themselves over many years through learning, reflection, practice, reasons, consequences, and moral education.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-07.proposition: An undamaged, informed, reasons-responsive, and self-controlled person can meaningfully be said to have been able to do otherwise despite deterministic causation.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source independently defines ordinary alternative-capacity through freedom from restraint, damage, deliberate misinformation, and impaired rational control, making the proposition a complete constructive criterion.

chunk-003:c003-02.proposition: Deliberate control by other agents differs responsibility-relevantly from impersonal natural causation because social institutions must address planned interpersonal interference that displaces another person's control.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source grounds the distinction in the social and political significance of other agents intentionally using their plans and projects to interfere with a person's activities and control.

chunk-003:c003-07.proposition: Public and proportionate punishment can sustain respect for law and instantiate a consequentialist notion of desert whose justification does not depend on whether determinism is true.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source positively grounds punishment in the good consequences of maintaining respected systems of law and proportionate sanctions, independently of the truth of determinism or indeterminism.

chunk-003:c003-10.proposition: Basic moral desert posits a nonexistent requirement, whereas the desert that matters is the familiar, conduct-sensitive everyday notion and is compatible with deterministic causation.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source expressly advances everyday comparative and conduct-sensitive desert as the operative positive conception and states that it is independent of whether determinism is true.

chunk-004:chunk004-c07.proposition: Consequentialist reasons can justify a rule-governed punishment system even though individual adjudication properly applies agreed rules rather than recalculating the consequences of punishment in each case.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source independently distinguishes the forward-looking justification of a legal practice from its stable internal administration and explains that case-specific calculation would undermine respect for law.

chunk-005:chunk-005-candidate-004.proposition: Although disappointment may appropriately guide children, serious wrongdoing by competent adults can justify moral anger that also warns others against comparable misconduct.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source draws a substantive age-and-competence distinction and positively defends moral anger toward grave adult wrongdoing as both fitting condemnation and a warning to others.
